strengths: Novel asymmetric cross-modal interaction mechanism that thoughtfully balances convergence speed and performance through modality-specific aligners (A2V and V2A with different temporal strategies)
Significant practical efficiency improvements: achieves strong results with 1.3M training samples vs. 30.7M for Ovi and 6.4M for UniVerse-1, demonstrating efficient cross-modal learning
Comprehensive multi-dimensional evaluation including audio quality (PQ, CU, WER), video quality (SC, DD, IQ), and audio-video consistency (LS, TC, EC) metrics
Thorough ablation studies validating each component (ACMI design, FAM effectiveness, MA-CFG impact, training strategies) with clear performance improvements
Strong generalization to out-of-distribution data: anime image example (Fig. 4b) shows clear advantages over Ovi and UniVerse-1 where competitors fail
Elegant unified framework supporting multiple audio-video tasks (joint generation, continuation, video-to-audio dubbing, audio-driven synthesis) without task-specific model designs
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, particularly Fig. 3 comparing interaction mechanisms and Fig. 4 showing qualitative results
Well-motivated technical contributions with clear articulation of limitations in prior work (global vs. symmetric temporal-aligned approaches)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty in individual components: dual-branch architecture directly adopts existing models (Wan 2.2-5B, 2.1-1.3B), cross-attention is standard, and mask prediction is straightforward. Novelty is primarily in combination and asymmetric interaction design

Small evaluation set (100 test samples, only 50 real-world) is insufficient for robust claims about generalization and competitive advantage; single OOD anime example inadequate for demonstrating OOD robustness
No user studies despite focus on synchronization and emotional consistency where human perception is critical; results rely entirely on automated metrics
LLM-based evaluation (Gemini-2.5-Pro) for timbre/emotion consistency is unvalidated with no inter-rater reliability reported; LLMs may have systematic biases and this approach lacks peer consensus

Reproducibility concerns: internally collected training dataset for Stage 2/3 not characterized (size, quality, accessibility); no code/model release plans mentioned; cannot fully verify experimental setup
Missing critical technical details: window size w for A2V context not specified, λm decay schedule undefined, task ratio selection (4:1:1:2:2) unjustified with no ablation study

Fairness of baseline comparisons: two-stage methods use different audio generation (F5-TTS), JavisDiT not designed for human speech, and UniVerse-1 performance anomalously poor (nearly static), suggesting possible implementation issues
Face-aware modulation assumes facial regions always dominate audio-video coupling; limited to human-centric scenarios with unclear generalization to other content types

No failure case analysis, no evaluation of content type performance variation, no computational cost comparisons, and missing sensitivity analyses (window size w, interpolation granularity, mask threshold effects)
Marginal improvements on some metrics: lip-sync (5.95 vs 6.48 for Ovi is worse), and some ablation improvements are small (Table 3: unsupervised FAM shows minimal difference from supervised)

strengths: Thoughtfully designed asymmetric cross-modal interaction mechanism that balances convergence speed and contextual information through modality-specific A2V and V2A aligners
Demonstrates significant training efficiency: achieves competitive results with 1.3M samples vs 30.7M for Ovi, a meaningful practical contribution
Comprehensive evaluation framework across audio quality, video quality, and audio-video consistency metrics with both in-distribution and out-of-distribution test cases
Thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3, Figures 5-7) systematically validating each architectural component and training strategy
Practical versatility: unifies five audio-video generation tasks in a single model, reducing need for task-specific designs
Clear presentation with effective architectural visualizations and justified design choices; well-motivated problem addressing limitations of existing decoupled pipelines
Shows robustness to out-of-distribution anime inputs where concurrent methods (Ovi) fail, indicating improved generalization
weaknesses: Critical evaluation concerns: timbre consistency (TC) and emotion consistency (EC)—core cross-modal alignment metrics—rely solely on LLM-based evaluation (Gemini-2.5-Pro) with no human validation, no inter-rater reliability analysis, and single evaluator system introducing potential biases

Limited technical novelty: individual components (cross-modal attention, face masks, CFG extensions) are not novel; asymmetric interaction is incremental engineering applying different context windows/interpolation—solid but not conceptually groundbreaking

Reproducibility severely compromised by internal unpublished dataset: no statistics provided on dataset size, duration, speaker diversity, or language variety, making results unreproducible and baseline comparisons potentially unfair

Incomplete experimental rigor: ablations conducted on first 10k of 30k training steps (different from full training), test set of only 100 samples, and OOD evaluation limited to anime without exploring other visual styles

Face-Aware Modulation lacks clarity: requires RetinaFace supervision at training but no explanation of inference-time application; marginal improvements (LS 3.89→4.09); decaying λ_m lacks principled justification; sensitive to face detection failures unaddressed

Training complexity without justification: three-stage pipeline with arbitrary task ratios (4:1:1:2:2), no ablation on these ratios; Figure 7 shows counterintuitive slower convergence for MTO vs JFML without adequate explanation

Incomplete technical analysis: no inference computational cost/speed reported, MA-CFG coefficients s_v and s_a lack ablation, lip-sync only via SyncNet without human assessment, sensitivity to hyperparameters unexplored

Scope limitations: 'human audio' focus restricted to speech only (singing, whispers unaddressed), generalization claims based on single anime example, dataset bias (speakers, languages, accents) not analyzed
Zero-initialization of W_o matrices (Eq. 7) is ad-hoc pragmatic solution lacking principled justification or ablation demonstrating necessity

strengths: Well-motivated asymmetric cross-modal interaction mechanism that balances convergence speed and performance through modal-specific designs (A2V with contextualized audio, V2A with temporal interpolation)
Practical multi-task unification framework handling joint generation, dubbing, audio-driven synthesis, and continuation within a single model, with demonstrated benefits from multi-task training
Impressive data efficiency: competitive results with 1.3M training samples versus 30.7M for competitors, suggesting effective architectural design

Comprehensive experimental validation including thorough ablation studies (Tables 2-3, 7-9), qualitative comparisons showing out-of-distribution generalization (anime inputs), and user study with 34 participants
Careful technical execution with thoughtful handling of temporal alignment, context windows, and component insertion positions; clear mathematical formulations
Effective presentation with informative figures, particularly Figure 3's conceptual comparison of interaction mechanisms
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core components (dual-branch, cross-attention, CFG) are standard; asymmetric interaction is incremental over symmetric temporal-aligned designs with modest empirical gains (LS: 3.73→4.09, TC: 0.685→0.725)

Serious evaluation methodology concerns: (1) Small test set (100 samples) without confidence intervals or significance testing; (2) Reliance on Gemini-2.5-Pro for key metrics (timbre/emotion consistency) lacks LLM validation, inter-rater reliability analysis, and systematic evaluation protocols; (3) These LLM metrics are differentiators from competitors but methodologically questionable

Major reproducibility limitations: private training dataset (Stage 2) prevents verification and fair comparison; reliance on proprietary Wan models for backbone; proprietary evaluation tools; no mentioned code/model release despite claims of addressing open-source limitations

Unfair dataset comparisons: different datasets with competitors (Ovi trained on 30.7M but dataset composition unknown); unclear sample counting (examples vs. tokens vs. frames); private Stage 2 data prevents reproducibility or validation of dataset characteristics

Constrained scope limiting generality: single-speaker human-centric only; cannot handle multi-person scenarios or ambient sounds; acknowledged but significantly narrows applicability compared to general audio-video generation claims
Face-aware modulation shows marginal gains (Table 3: LS 3.89→4.09) with added complexity requiring ground-truth mask annotations; context window w=1/2 lacks justification or ablation study

Ablation studies use early training stages (first 10k steps of Stage 2) rather than final models, undermining conclusions about component contributions; MA-CFG shows trade-offs in image quality despite consistency improvements (Table 9)

Inconsistent quantitative results undercutting main claims: UniAVGen underperforms Ovi on lip-sync (LS: 5.95 vs 6.48) despite synchronized generation claims; public benchmark results (Tables 5-6) show near-SOTA rather than clear superiority

Statistical rigor absent: no error bars, confidence intervals, or significance tests in Table 1; user study lacks statistical analysis; no inter-rater agreement metrics for LLM evaluations; no sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters

Unclear contribution attribution: backbone models (Wan 2.2-5B, Wan 2.1-1.3B) are pre-trained; uncertain how much improvement derives from proposed components versus pre-training quality; total training steps modest (200k total)
